newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Rifkind denies China already runs Hong Kong. [CORRECTED 15:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Rifkind denies China already runs Hong Kong. [CORRECTED 15:00 GMT]

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind rejected claims that China had already assumed de facto power in Hong Kong and that Britain should accede to Beijing's wishes for the territory.
"I completely reject this approach," a prepared text of Rifkind's dinner speech distributed to journalists prior to delivery on Sunday. (Corrects day of speech to Sunday from Saturday.)

Rifkind, in Hong Kong on a weekend visit, said the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration governing the handover of Hong Kong committed Britain to ruling the colony for the next 19 weeks until the stroke of midnight on June 30, 1997 and that it would discharge that obligation.
"Even if we wanted to, we could not put Hong Kong on stand-by for six months while we tried to sort out matters with the Chinese."

Britain and China are at loggerheads over China's plans to replace Hong Kong's elected legislature with an interim appointed chamber and dilute some of the territory's civil liberties laws after Hong Kong is handed back to China on July 1 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
Hong Kong politician David Chu earlier summed up the pro-Beijing camp's views, accusing the British of interfering in affairs that were China's responsibility.
"The British government should face the reality to cooperate with China -- that's the most wise decision," Chu said in a statement titled "Good-bye, Rifkind!" faxed to the media.

"Hong Kong people running Hong Kong is truly beginning. Britain now does not rule Hong Kong anymore. If the British plays any more tricks, it would only be a waste of time," said the fax, sent a day before Rifkind's arrival on Saturday.
The pro-democracy camp, on the other hand, has accused Britain of not doing enough to preserve Hong Kong's rights.
Rifkind said London's responsibility would not end with the handover and Britain would not withdraw to the sidelines as a mere spectator.

The Joint Declaration binds China to preserve Hong Kong's freedoms and capitalist way of life for another 50 years. Rifkind said Britain would monitor events in territory after the handover and report to parliament every six months on whether China was honouring that pledge.
"Hong Kong will remain Britain's business for long after the handover. That is our wish and our pledge."
